row.Question:
What is the next step in a patient with atrial fibrillation, palpitations, and unknown thyroid status?
a) Prescribe beta-blocker immediately
b) Measure TSH levels
c) Start anticoagulants
d) Refer for cardioversion
e) Do coronary angiography
row.Reference: Kirchhof, P., Camm, A. J., Goette, N., Brandes, L. F., Eckardt, M., & Esc Group. (2016). 2016 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation developed in collaboration with EACTS. European Heart Journal
row.Context: Screening for underlying causes of atrial fibrillation (AF) is recommended for all patients, including measurement of thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) levels to exclude hyperthyroidism, and a thorough history and physical examination to exclude structural heart disease."

row.Question:
What is the target LDL cholesterol level in patients with cardiovascular disease?
a) Below 2.5 mmol/L
b) Below 2.0 mmol/L
c) Below 1.5 mmol/L
d) Above 3.0 mmol/L
e) Exactly 2.0 mmol/L
row.Reference: LDL-cholesterol targets as Achilles' heel of 2020 ISH guidelines - PMC - PubMed
row.Context: The 2019 ESC/EAS Guidelines for the management of dyslipidaemias introduced even the concept of “extreme high risk group”, stating, that in some patients who experience a second vascular event within 2 years (not necessarily of the same type as the first event) while taking maximally tolerated statin-based therapy, an LDL-cholesterol goal of <1.0 mmol/L (40 mg/dL) is recommended. For the broader "very high risk" category (which includes all patients with established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease), the LDL-cholesterol target is <1.4 mmol/L (55 mg/dL).

row.Question:
What is the most common cause of chest pain not related to ischemia?
a) Angina pectoris
b) Pericarditis
c) Musculoskeletal chest wall pain
d) Pulmonary embolism
e) Aortic dissection
row.Reference: Chest Pain - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Musculoskeletal chest pain, including costochondritis and Tietze's syndrome, is the most common cause of non-cardiac chest pain.

row.Question:
What is the first step in managing a patient with a suspected pulmonary edema?
a) Oral antibiotics
b) Oxygen therapy and diuretics
c) Corticosteroids
d) Inhalers
e) Bronchoscopy
row.Reference: Acute Pulmonary Edema - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The initial management of acute pulmonary edema should focus on stabilization of the patient's condition. This includes oxygen therapy and the administration of diuretics

row.Question:
What is the diagnostic hallmark of atrial fibrillation on ECG?
a) ST elevation
b) Absence of P waves and irregular R-R intervals
c) Long QT interval
d) Fixed AV block
e) Normal sinus rhythm
row.Text Answer: Absence of P waves and irregular R-R intervals
row.Reference: Kirchhof, P., Camm, A. J., Goette, N., Brandes, L. F., Eckardt, L., & Endrich, B. (2016). 2016 ESC Guidelines for the management of atrial fibrillation developed in collaboration with EACTS. European Heart Journal, 37(38)
row.Context: he diagnostic hallmark of atrial fibrillation (AF) on the electrocardiogram (ECG) is irregularly irregular R-R intervals and the absence of discernible P waves, with the presence of fibrillatory waves varying in morphology and amplitude.

row.Question:
Which antihypertensive class is also used to treat benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH)?
a) Beta blockers
b) ACE inhibitors
c) Alpha blockers
d) Calcium channel blockers
e) Diuretics
row.Reference: Roehrborn, C. G., & Schwinn, D. A. (2004). Alpha1-adrenergic receptors and their antagonists in the treatment of lower urinary tract symptoms and benign prostatic hyperplasia. Journal of Urology, 171(3),
row.Context: Alpha-blockers are a class of medications that are effective in treating both hypertension and symptoms of benign prostatic hyperplasia (BPH) due to their ability to relax smooth muscle in the prostate and bladder neck, as well as in peripheral blood vessels.

row.Question:
What is the most common pathogen causing traveler’s diarrhea?
a) Rotavirus
b) Salmonella
c) Escherichia coli (E. coli)
d) Giardia lamblia
e) Shigella
row.Reference: Travelers Diarrhea - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The most common bacterial cause is enterotoxigenic Escherichia coli (ETEC), with estimates that the bacteria is responsible for nearly 30% of cases.

row.Question:
What is the most effective non-drug intervention for allergic rhinitis?
a) Corticosteroids
b) Allergen avoidance
c) Antihistamines
d) Decongestants
e) Saline nasal rinses
row.Reference: Bousquet, J., Khaltaev, N., Cruz, A. A., Denburg, J., Fokkens, W. J., Togias, C., ... & White, P. (2008). Allergic Rhinitis and its Impact on Asthma (ARIA) 2008 update (in collaboration with the World Health Organization, GA(2)LEN and AllerGen). Allergy, 63(Suppl. 86),
row.Context: The primary and most effective non-pharmacological intervention for allergic rhinitis is allergen avoidance. This involves reducing exposure to identified allergens (e.g., dust mites, pet dander, pollen) in the environment.

row.Question:
What is the correct action for a nosebleed at home?
a) Tilt head back and lie down
b) Sit upright, pinch the soft part of the nose, and lean forward
c) Apply warm compress to the neck
d) Drink warm fluids
e) Use antihistamines
row.Text Answer: Sit upright, pinch the soft part of the nose, and lean forward
row.Reference: Nosebleed - Mayo Clinic.
row.Context:
.To stop a nosebleed:

Sit upright and lean forward slightly. This will prevent blood from running down the back of your throat.
Pinch the soft part of your nose (just above the nostrils) firmly and continuously for at least 10 to 15 minutes.

row.Question:
A patient presents with vertical gaze palsy. Which brain structure is most likely affected?
a) Pons
b) Dorsal midbrain (mesencephalon)
c) Internal capsule
d) Basal ganglia
e) Thalamus
row.Reference: Vertical Gaze Palsy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Disorders of vertical gaze commonly result from lesions of the dorsal midbrain (also known as the pretectal area), where the vertical gaze centers and the interstitial nucleus of Cajal are located. Parinaud syndrome, a classic example of dorsal midbrain syndrome, typically includes vertical gaze palsy.

row.Question:
A lesion of the left medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) will result in:
a) Impaired abduction of the right eye during leftward gaze
b) Impaired adduction of the left eye during rightward gaze, with nystagmus of the right eye
c) Complete bilateral ophthalmoplegia
d) Vertical gaze palsy
e) Impaired convergence
row.Text Answer: Impaired adduction of the left eye during rightward gaze, with nystagmus of the right eye
row.Reference: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: A lesion of the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF) on one side, such as the left MLF, results in an internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO). This is characterized by impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye (e.g., the left eye fails to adduct when looking to the right) and nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye (e.g., nystagmus of the right eye when looking to the right).

row.Question:
A man with ataxia on one side of the body, dysarthria, ipsilateral Horner’s syndrome, and contralateral body sensory loss most likely has:
a) Medial medullary syndrome
b) Weber syndrome
c) Wallenberg syndrome (PICA infarct)
d) Benedikt syndrome
e) Locked-in syndrome
row.Reference: Wallenberg Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Wallenberg syndrome, also known as lateral medullary syndrome, typically results from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or its branches. Its characteristic features include ipsilateral cerebellar signs (ataxia), dysarthria, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body

row.Question:
24. A patient is unable to repeat spoken words but speaks fluently and understands language. What type of aphasia is this?
a) Broca's aphasia
b) Wernicke’s aphasia
c) Conduction aphasia
d) Transcortical sensory aphasia
e) Global aphasia
row.Reference: Wallenberg Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Wallenberg syndrome, also known as lateral medullary syndrome, typically results from occlusion of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA) or its branches. Its characteristic features include ipsilateral cerebellar signs (ataxia), dysarthria, ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation over the body.

row.Question:
What is the first imaging method in a patient who presents with sudden onset hemiparesis and gaze deviation?
a) Non-contrast head CT
b) Brain MRI with contrast
c) Spinal MRI
d) EEG
e) Angiography
row.Reference: Powers, W. J., Rabinstein, A. A., Telegrafo, T. H., et al. (2019). Guidelines for the Early Management of Patients With Acute Ischemic Stroke: 2019 Update to the 2018 Guidelines for the Early Management of Acute Ischemic Stroke. Stroke, 50(12)
row.Context: For patients presenting with acute neurological deficits suggestive of stroke (such as sudden onset hemiparesis and gaze deviation), non-contrast head CT (NCCT) is the recommended first-line imaging modality. Its primary purpose is to rapidly differentiate between ischemic stroke and hemorrhagic stroke, which guides acute management decisions.

row.Question:
What is the hallmark of internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO)?
a) Bilateral abduction deficit
b) Vertical gaze limitation with nystagmus
c) Impaired adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye
d) Bilateral ptosis and mydriasis
e) Downward gaze paralysis
row.Text Answer: Impaired adduction of one eye with nystagmus of the abducting eye
row.Reference: Internuclear Ophthalmoplegia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) is a disorder of conjugate horizontal gaze resulting from a lesion in the medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). The hallmark features are impaired adduction of the ipsilateral eye (on attempted lateral gaze) and nystagmus of the contralateral abducting eye."

row.Question:
Which neurological condition is characterized by constructional apraxia and dressing apraxia due to damage in the non-dominant parietal lobe?
a) Wernicke’s aphasia
b) Hemispatial neglect syndrome
c) Broca’s aphasia
d) Parkinson’s disease
e) Optic ataxia
row.Reference: Hemispatial Neglect - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Lesions of the non-dominant (typically right) parietal lobe can lead to a constellation of deficits known as hemispatial neglect syndrome. This syndrome is characterized by a failure to attend to stimuli on the contralateral side of space, and it often includes constructional apraxia (difficulty drawing or building) and dressing apraxia (difficulty organizing and performing the motor actions necessary for dressing).

row.Question:
A patient presents with tongue deviation to the left and atrophy on that side. Where is the lesion?
a) Right cerebral cortex
b) Left facial nerve nucleus
c) Left hypoglossal nerve
d) Right corticospinal tract
e) Right vagus nerve
row.Reference: Hypoglossal Nerve Palsy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: A lesion of the hypoglossal nerve (cranial nerve XII) leads to weakness, atrophy, and fasciculations of the ipsilateral half of the tongue. When the patient is asked to protrude the tongue, it will deviate towards the side of the lesion due to the unopposed action of the healthy genioglossus muscle on the contralateral side.

row.Question:
What is the characteristic gait of a patient with normotensive hydrocephalus?
a) Steppage gait
b) Waddling gait
c) Ataxic gait
d) Magnetic (marche à petits pas) gait
e) Festinating gait
row.Reference: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: The gait disturbance in normal pressure hydrocephalus (NPH) is often characterized by a 'magnetic' gait, also known as 'marche à petits pas' (gait of small steps). Patients appear as though their feet are glued to the floor, with difficulty lifting their feet, a wide base, and impaired balance, despite a lack of significant weakness.

row.Question:
Which cranial nerve is not located in the cavernous sinus?
a) CN III
b) CN IV
c) CN V1
d) CN VI
e) CN II
row.Reference: Cavernous Sinus Anatomy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The cavernous sinus contains several important neurovascular structures. The cranial nerves passing through the cavernous sinus are the oculomotor nerve (CN III), the trochlear nerve (CN IV), the ophthalmic division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V1), the maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V2), and the abducens nerve (CN VI). The optic nerve (CN II) does not pass through the cavernous sinus; it travels directly from the orbit to the optic chiasm.

row.Question:
What neurological sign is seen in a patient who climbs up their thighs with their hands to stand up from the floor?
a) Lhermitte’s sign
b) Gowers' sign
c) Romberg sign
d) Froment sign
e) Babinski sign
row.Reference: Gowers Sign - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Gowers' sign is a classic clinical finding observed in patients with proximal muscle weakness, particularly in Duchenne muscular dystrophy. It is characterized by the patient's difficulty rising from a sitting or supine position on the floor, requiring them to "climb up" their own legs with their hands to achieve an upright posture.

row.Question:
What syndrome results from a lesion affecting the corticospinal tract and CN III in the midbrain?
a) Wallenberg syndrome
b) Benedikt syndrome
c) Weber syndrome
d) Locked-in syndrome
e) Medial medullary syndrome
row.Reference: Weber Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Weber syndrome is a midbrain stroke syndrome resulting from a lesion affecting the cerebral peduncle (containing the corticospinal and corticobulbar tracts) and the exiting fibers of the oculomotor nerve (CN III). Clinically, it presents as ipsilateral oculomotor nerve palsy (ptosis, dilated pupil, eye deviated down and out) and contralateral hemiplegia (weakness) due to damage to the corticospinal tract

row.Question:
Which structure is primarily involved in recognizing faces?
a) Angular gyrus
b) Broca's area
c) Fusiform gyrus
d) Prefrontal cortex
e) Parahippocampal gyrus
row.Reference: Prosopagnosia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: The fusiform gyrus (located in the inferior temporal lobe) contains the fusiform face area (FFA), a region that shows particularly strong activation when individuals view faces. It is widely considered to be a key region involved in the processing and recognition of faces. Damage to this area can lead to prosopagnosia (face blindness)

row.Question:
Which gait is associated with peroneal nerve palsy?
a) Festinating gait
b) Steppage (high stepping) gait
c) Ataxic gait
d) Waddling gait
e) Spastic scissoring gait
row.Reference: Peroneal Nerve Injury - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The most common presentation of common peroneal nerve injury is a weakness of ankle dorsiflexion leading to the classic foot drop, which often causes patients to catch their toes on the ground while ambulating or ambulate with a high steppage gait to prevent dragging their toes on the ground.

row.Question:
What is the most appropriate imaging for suspected spinal cord compression with sensory level at the nipples (T4)?
a) Brain MRI
b) Lumbar puncture
c) Cervical spine X-ray
d) Thoracic spine MRI
e) Thoracic CT without contrast
row.Reference: Spinal Cord Compression - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: When spinal cord compression is suspected, particularly with a localized sensory level, magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the relevant spinal region is the imaging modality of choice. MRI provides superior visualization of the spinal cord, nerve roots, intervertebral discs, and surrounding soft tissues, allowing for precise localization and characterization of the compressive lesion. Given a sensory level at the nipples, the thoracic spine is the targeted region

row.Question:
What neurological disorder is characterized by increased muscle tone, brisk reflexes, and extensor plantar response?
a) Lower motor neuron lesion
b) Upper motor neuron lesion
c) Neuropathy
d) Myopathy
e) Cerebellar syndrome
row.Reference: Upper Motor Neuron Lesion - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Lesions of the upper motor neuron (UMN) pathway typically result in a characteristic constellation of clinical signs including increased muscle tone (spasticity), brisk deep tendon reflexes, and the presence of pathological reflexes such as the extensor plantar response (Babinski sign).

row.Question:
Which type of aphasia is most likely if the patient speaks fluently, uses neologisms, cannot understand language, but can repeat?
a) Broca’s aphasia
b) Transcortical sensory aphasia
c) Conduction aphasia
d) Global aphasia
e) Wernicke’s aphasia
row.Reference: Aphasia - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Transcortical sensory aphasia is characterized by fluent speech, often with paraphasias and neologisms, and severe impairment of auditory comprehension. The distinguishing feature, however, is the preserved ability to repeat words and phrases, despite the comprehension deficit

row.Question:
A patient has right hemiparesis and conjugate eye deviation to the left. Where is the lesion?
a) Left frontal eye field
b) Left parietal lobe
c) Right brainstem
d) Right occipital lobe
e) Left cerebellar hemisphere
row.Text Answer: patient has right hemiparesis and conjugate eye deviation to the left. Where is the lesion?
row.Reference: Gaze Palsies - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Lesions affecting the frontal eye fields (located in the frontal lobe) cause a deviation of the eyes toward the side of the lesion and away from the side of the hemiparesis. Thus, a lesion in the left frontal eye field would lead to conjugate gaze deviation to the left and right-sided hemiparesis due to the involvement of the adjacent motor cortex.

row.Question:
What is a classic symptom of Friedreich’s ataxia outside the nervous system?
a) Hepatic failure
b) Cardiomyopathy
c) Cataract
d) Retinopathy
e) Cushingoid face
row.Reference: Clinical Features of Friedreich Ataxia - PMC - PubMed Central.
row.Context: Friedreich's ataxia is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder, but it is also associated with significant non-neurological manifestations. The most common and clinically relevant extra-neurological finding is cardiomyopathy (abnormal thickening of the heart muscle), which often leads to heart failure and is a leading cause of mortality in affected individuals. Other common non-neurological issues include skeletal deformities (e.g., scoliosis, pes cavus) and diabetes mellitus..

row.Question:
What is the mechanism of Wallerian degeneration?
a) Retrograde axonal degeneration
b) Segmental demyelination
c) Anterograde axonal degeneration distal to the injury
d) Neuronal apoptosis in the cortex
e) Mitochondrial toxicity
row.Text Answer: Anterograde axonal degeneration distal to the injury
row.Reference: Wallerian Degeneration - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Wallerian degeneration is an active process of anterograde axonal degeneration that occurs in the portion of an axon distal to a site of injury. It involves the breakdown of the axon and its myelin sheath after the axon has been severed or crushed, leading to the disintegration of the distal segment of the nerve fiber

row.Question:
What symptom combination is typical for transtentorial uncal herniation?
a) Bilateral miosis and aphasia
b) Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis
c) Bilateral vision loss and normal consciousness
d) Diplopia and central scotoma
e) Hypotension and coma
row.Text Answer: Ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil and contralateral hemiparesis
row.Reference: Brain Herniation - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Uncal herniation, a type of transtentorial herniation, typically results in compression of the ipsilateral oculomotor nerve (CN III) and the contralateral cerebral peduncle. This leads to a classic clinical triad of ipsilateral (same side) pupillary dilation and unresponsiveness to light (fixed and dilated pupil) due to parasympathetic fiber compression, and contralateral (opposite side) hemiparesis or hemiplegia from the compression of the corticospinal tract

row.Question:
A patient presents with anosognosia and hemispatial neglect. Where is the lesion?
a) Dominant parietal lobe
b) Dominant frontal lobe
c) Occipital cortex
d) Non-dominant parietal lobe
e) Basal ganglia
row.Reference: Hemispatial Neglect - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Hemispatial neglect (or unilateral spatial neglect) is a disorder of attention characterized by a failure to report or respond to stimuli presented on the side opposite to the brain lesion. It is most frequently caused by damage to the non-dominant (typically right) parietal lobe. This region's involvement often also leads to anosognosia, which is the patient's unawareness or denial of their own neurological deficit, such as their hemiparesis or neglect.

row.Question:
1. Which of the following enzymes is directly involved in the iodination of tyrosyl residues in thyroglobulin within the thyroid follicle lumen?
a) Iodotyrosine deiodinase
b) Thyroid peroxidase
c) 5’-deiodinase type 2
d) Tyrosine hydroxylase
row.Reference: de Vijlder, J. J. M., & Bikker, R. (2000). Biochemistry and physiology of thyroid peroxidase. In D. P. Nauseef (Ed.), The Peroxidase Multigene Family of Enzymes (pp. 117–132). Springer.
row.Context: “Thyroglobulin is the protein in which iodine, bound to tyrosine residues, and thyroid hormone, formed from these iodinated tyrosine residues, is stored until needed. Iodination and coupling of iodo-tyrosine residues is catalyzed by the enzyme thyroid peroxidase (TPO) within the colloid of the thyroid follicle.”

row.Question:
2. Parathyroid hormone (PTH) exerts its effects via which intracellular second messenger pathway in renal tubular cells?
a) IP3/DAG cascade only
b) cAMP-dependent protein kinase A
c) Direct G-protein coupled activation of phospholipase C
d) Activation of nuclear steroid receptors
row.Reference: Sutkeviciute, I., Jean-Alphonse, F. G., & Vilardaga, J.-P. (2017). Endosomal PTH Receptor Signaling Through cAMP and Its Consequence for Human Medicine. In Structure and Function of GPCRs (pp. 181–193). Springer.
row.Context: "The parathyroid hormone (PTH) type 1 receptor (PTHR) is a medically important G protein-coupled receptor (GPCR) that triggers the cAMP/PKA signaling pathway in kidney and bone cells to regulate calcium ion homeostasis and bone turnover."

row.Question:
3. The MEN1 tumor suppressor gene product, menin, interacts directly with which nuclear complex?
a) Retinoblastoma (Rb) complex
b) mTOR complex 1
c) MLL (Mixed Lineage Leukemia) histone methyltransferase complex
d) APC complex
row.Text Answer: MLL (Mixed Lineage Leukemia) histone methyltransferase complex
row.Reference: Yokoyama, A., Wang, Z., Wysocka, J., Sanyal, M., Aufiero, D. J., Kitabayashi, I., Herr, W., & Cleary, M. L. (2004). Leukemia proto‐oncoprotein MLL forms a SET1‐like histone methyltransferase complex with menin to regulate Hox gene expression. Molecular and Cellular Biology, 24(13), 5639–5649.
row.Context: “Menin, a product of the MEN1 tumor suppressor gene, is also a component of the 1‐MDa MLL complex. Abrogation of menin expression phenocopies loss of MLL and reveals a critical role for menin in the maintenance of Hox gene expression. Oncogenic mutant forms of MLL retain an ability to interact with menin but not other identified complex components. These studies link the menin tumor suppressor protein with the MLL histone methyltransferase machinery, with implications for Hox gene expression in development and leukemia pathogenesis.”

row.Question:
4. In patients with sight-threatening thyroid eye disease who are unresponsive to glucocorticoids, the next step in therapy is:
a) Rituximab
b) Mycophenolate mofetil
c) Orbital radiotherapy
d) Teprotumumab (IGF-1R inhibitor monoclonal antibody)
row.Reference: Ugradar, S., Malkhasyan, E., & Douglas, R. S. (2024). Teprotumumab for the Treatment of Thyroid Eye Disease. Endocrine Reviews, 45(3), bnae018.
row.Context: "Teprotumumab, a fully human IgG1 monoclonal antibody that inhibits the IGF-1R, recently gained approval in the United States for the treatment of TED. In phase 2 and phase 3 clinical studies, teprotumumab showed efficacy in reducing inflammation, proptosis, diplopia, and burden on quality of life in patients who were treated. Postintroduction studies have confirmed the results of the phase 2 and phase 3 studies. Since 2020, more than 5800 patients have been treated with teprotumumab, and it appears to be well tolerated. The American Thyroid Association and the European Thyroid Association have recommended it as first-line therapy for patients with moderate to severe TED who display features of proptosis and diplopia."

row.Question:
5. A mutation in which gene is most commonly associated with generalized glucocorticoid resistance (Chrousos syndrome)?
a) NR3C1 (glucocorticoid receptor gene)
b) POMC
c) HSD11B1
d) CYP11B1
row.Reference: Charmandari, E., Kino, T., Ichijo, T., & Chrousos, G. P. (2008). Generalized glucocorticoid resistance: Clinical aspects, molecular mechanisms, and implications of a rare genetic disorder. The Journal of Clinical Endocrinology & Metabolism, 93(5), 1563–1572.
row.Context: “Primary generalized glucocorticoid resistance (Chrousos syndrome) is a rare genetic disorder characterized by impaired sensitivity of all target tissues to glucocorticoids. This syndrome results from heterozygous, loss‐of‐function mutations in the human glucocorticoid receptor (hGR) gene (NR3C1) located on chromosome 5q31–32. To date, over 30 different NR3C1 mutations—most of which disrupt ligand binding or DNA‐binding functions of the receptor—have been identified in affected patients. These inactivating NR3C1 mutations reduce feedback inhibition at the level of the hypothalamus and pituitary, leading to compensatory increases in ACTH secretion and resultant elevations in adrenal steroid production.”

row.Question:
6. Metyrapone inhibits the synthesis of cortisol by blocking which enzyme?
a) 21-hydroxylase
b) 11β-hydroxylase
c) 17α-hydroxylase
d) Aldosterone synthase
row.Reference: Pivonello, R., De Leo, M., Cozzolino, A., & Colao, A. (2021). Metyrapone in Cushing’s syndrome: a profile of its use. Drugs & Therapy Perspectives, 37(3), 109–117.
row.Context: "Metyrapone and its active metabolite, metyrapol, dose-dependently inhibit the two highly homologous isoforms of 11-hydroxylase, 11β-hydroxylase (CYP11B1) and 18-hydroxylase (CYP11B2), and consequently inhibit cortisol and aldosterone production."

row.Question:
7. Which subunit of the insulin receptor has intrinsic tyrosine kinase activity?
a) α-subunit
b) β-subunit
c) IRS-1
d) PI3K
row.Reference: Ullrich, A., Bell, G. I., Chen, E. Y., Herrera, R., Petruzzelli, L. M., Dull, T. J., ... & Taylor, S. I. (1985). Human insulin receptor and its relationship to the receptor for insulin‐like growth factor I. Nature, 313(6005), 756–761.
row.Context: “The insulin receptor is synthesized as a single polypeptide that is proteolytically cleaved into two disulfide-linked subunits: an extracellular α-subunit and a transmembrane β-subunit. The β-subunit contains an intrinsic tyrosine kinase domain responsible for the receptor’s autophosphorylation and downstream signalling activity.”

row.Question:
8. In 17α-hydroxylase deficiency, the following profile is typical:
a) Low cortisol, low mineralocorticoids, low androgens
b) Low cortisol, high mineralocorticoids, low androgens
c) High cortisol, high mineralocorticoids, high androgens
d) High cortisol, low mineralocorticoids, high androgens
row.Text Answer: Low cortisol, high mineralocorticoids, low androgens
row.Reference: Medscape. (n.d.). 17-Hydroxylase Deficiency Syndrome.
row.Context: "17-hydroxylase (17-OH) deficiency syndrome is a rare genetic disorder of steroid biosynthesis that causes decreased production of glucocorticoids and sex steroids by the adrenal glands and increased synthesis of mineralocorticoid precursors."

row.Question:
9. Octreotide’s mechanism in treating acromegaly primarily involves:
a) Directly binding to GH-receptors
b) Inhibiting GHRH secretion
c) Mimicking somatostatin to suppress GH secretion
d) Increasing GH receptor degradation
row.Text Answer: Mimicking somatostatin to suppress GH secretion
row.Reference: Melmed, S. (2005). Medical progress: Acromegaly. The New England Journal of Medicine, 355(24), 2558–2573.
row.Context: “Somatostatin analogs such as octreotide bind primarily to somatostatin receptor subtype 2 (SSTR2) on pituitary somatotrophs, leading to inhibition of adenylyl cyclase, reduced intracellular cAMP, and consequent suppression of growth‐hormone release.”

row.Question:
10. The defect in pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1a involves which protein?
a) α-subunit of Gs-protein (GNAS1 mutation)
b) PTH receptor (PTHR1)
c) Calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR)
d) Vitamin D receptor
row.Reference: Kotanidou, E. P., Tsinopoulou, V.-R., Serbis, A., Litou, E., & Galli-Tsinopoulou, A. (2021). Pseudohypoparathyroidism Type 1A with Normocalcaemia, due to the Novel c.389A>G (p.Tyr130Cys) Mutation in the GNAS Gene. Journal of Bone Metabolism, 28(1), 85–89.
row.Context: "Pseudohypoparathyroidism type 1A (PHP1A) is a rare disease caused by molecular defects in the maternally-inherited allele of the guanine nucleotide-binding protein, α-stimulating (GNAS) gene. The GNAS gene encodes the stimulatory G-protein α-subunit that regulates production of the second messenger cyclic adenosine monophosphate."

row.Question:
1. The use of digitalis and verapamil is absolutely contraindicated in:
a. Atrial fibrillation
b. Atrial flutter
c. Atrial tachycardia
d. Atrial extrasystoles
e. Atrial fibrillation in a patient with WPW‐type preexcitation

In addition to vessels, CT often effectively visualizes and distinguishes between reversible and irreversible changes in the bowel wall.

b. CD20 positivity by IHC → BCL2 rearrangement by FISH → R-CHOP therapy
c. CD30 positivity by IHC, followed by ALK IHC staining → if ALK IHC positive, do ALK break-apart FISH → if negative, test for DUSP22 and TP63 rearrangements
d. Ki-67 staining → determine proliferation index; if > 60 %, treat as ALK-positive
e. EBV-encoded RNA in situ hybridization; if positive, label as ALK-positive
row.Text Answer: CD30 positivity by IHC, followed by ALK IHC staining → if ALK IHC positive, do ALK break-apart FISH → if negative, test for DUSP22 and TP63 rearrangements
row.Reference: Bennani‐Baiti, N., Ansell, S., & Feldman, A. L. (2016). Adult systemic anaplastic large‐cell lymphoma: Recommendations for diagnosis and management. Expert Review of Hematology, 9(2), 137–150.

row.Question:
4. In the linear-quadratic model (α/β model), which describes late-responding tissues and how do you calculate BED for 2 Gy × 30 fractions vs. 2.5 Gy × 25 fractions when α/β = 3 Gy?
a. α – single-hit, β – double-hit; BED₂Gy×30 = 100 Gy₃; BED₂.₅Gy×25 = 114.6 Gy₃
b. α – repopulation, β – repair; BED₂Gy×30 = 90 Gy₃; BED₂.₅Gy×25 = 110 Gy₃
c. α – repair, β – repopulation; BED₂Gy×30 = 80 Gy₃; BED₂.₅Gy×25 = 120 Gy₃
d. α – oxygen effect, β – reoxygenation; BED₂Gy×30 = 100 Gy₁₀; BED₂.₅Gy×25 = 115 Gy₁₀
e. α – fractionation, β – fraction size; BED₂Gy×30 = 100 Gy₃; BED₂.₅Gy×25 = 125 Gy₃
row.Text Answer: α – single-hit, β – double-hit; BED₂Gy×30 = 100 Gy₃; BED₂.₅Gy×25 = 114.6 Gy₃
row.Reference: Biologically Effective Dose (BED) Calculator. (n.d.). MDApp.
row.Context:
“The Biologically Effective Dose (BED) is a measure of the true biological dose delivered by a particular combination of dose per fraction and total dose to a particular tissue characterized by a specific α/β ratio and is commonly used for isoeffective dose calculations.
“An α/β ratio of 10 is typically used for early‐responding tissues and tumors whilst an α/β ratio of 3 is often used for late‐responding tissues, such as normal tissue.
“The formulas used, based on the linear dependence of cell survival, are:
BED = Total dose × (1 + Fraction dose / α/β)” 
Calculation for late‐responding tissues (α/β = 3 Gy):
2 Gy × 30 fractions:
– Total dose = 2 Gy × 30 = 60 Gy
– BED = 60 × (1 + 2/3) = 60 × 1.6667 = 100 Gy₃
2.5 Gy × 25 fractions:
– Total dose = 2.5 Gy × 25 = 62.5 Gy
– BED = 62.5 × (1 + 2.5/3) = 62.5 × 1.8333 ≈ 114.6 Gy₃“

b) Parinaud’s syndrome (dorsal midbrain syndrome)

row.Context: Parinaud’s syndrome, also known as the dorsal midbrain syndrome, is a classic neurological condition resulting from a lesion in the dorsal midbrain (pretectal area). row.Question:
A patient with hemiplegia and complete facial palsy on the contralateral side likely has a lesion where?
a) Internal capsule
b) Cerebral cortex
c) Brainstem (pons)
d) Cerebellum
e) Spinal cord

row.Context: Lesions within the brainstem, particularly in the pons, commonly produce crossed syndromes. These are characterized by an ipsilateral (same-sided) cranial nerve deficit (such as a complete facial palsy due to involvement of the facial nerve nucleus or its fibers) and a contralateral (opposite-sided) hemiparesis or hemiplegia due to disruption of the descending corticospinal tracts before their decussation in the medulla

row.Question:
Which combination of symptoms best localizes a lesion to the cerebellopontine angle?
a) Facial droop, limb weakness, hemianopia
b) Ipsilateral facial paralysis, sensorineural hearing loss, and absent corneal reflex
c) Diplopia, dysarthria, dysphagia
d) Contralateral hemiparesis and aphasia
e) Vertical gaze palsy and internuclear ophthalmoplegia
row.Text Answer: Ipsilateral facial paralysis, sensorineural hearing loss, and absent corneal reflex
row.Reference: Vestibular Schwannoma (Acoustic Neuroma) - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Lesions affecting the cerebellopontine angle (CPA), such as acoustic neuromas (vestibular schwannomas), typically present with a characteristic constellation of cranial nerve deficits due to the close proximity of several nerves in this region. The most common early symptom is ipsilateral sensorineural hearing loss (CN VIII). As the lesion grows, it often compresses the adjacent facial nerve (CN VII), leading to ipsilateral facial weakness or paralysis, and the trigeminal nerve (CN V), resulting in ipsilateral facial numbness or an absent corneal reflex.

row.Question:
What is the pathophysiological mechanism behind Marcus Gunn pupil?
a) Parasympathetic overactivation
b) Relative afferent pupillary defect due to optic nerve damage
c) Midbrain tectal lesion
d) Sympathetic overactivity
e) Compression of CN III nucleus
row.Text Answer: Relative afferent pupillary defect due to optic nerve damage
row.Reference: Marcus Gunn Pupil - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: A Marcus Gunn pupil, also known as a relative afferent pupillary defect (RAPD), is an abnormal pupillary response that signifies a relative weakness of the afferent limb of the pupillary light reflex in one eye compared to the other. This is typically caused by a lesion of the optic nerve (pre-chiasmal) or severe, asymmetric retinal disease, leading to a reduced signal sent from the affected eye to the brain in response to light.

row.Question:
What is the most probable diagnosis in a 77-year-old woman with acute bilateral blindness and asymmetric paraparesis with a T4 sensory level?
a) Bilateral occipital infarcts
b) Multiple sclerosis
c) Anterior spinal artery syndrome
d) Neuromyelitis optica (Devic's disease)
e) Alzheimer's disease
row.Reference: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Neuromyelitis optica (NMO), also known as Devic's disease, is a severe autoimmune astrocytopathy that primarily affects the central nervous system, with a predilection for the optic nerves and spinal cord. Its hallmark clinical manifestations are acute, severe optic neuritis (which can be bilateral and lead to blindness) and acute transverse myelitis (resulting in motor weakness like paraparesis, sensory loss with a distinct sensory level, and bladder/bowel dysfunction). The simultaneous or sequential occurrence of these severe attacks is characteristic of NMO.

row.Question:
What syndrome presents with one-and-a-half eye movement abnormality (one eye can only abduct, the other cannot move horizontally)?
a) Parinaud’s syndrome
b) Horner’s syndrome
c) Lesion of PPRF and MLF (one-and-a-half syndrome)
d) Lateral medullary syndrome
e) Oculomotor nerve palsy
row.Text Answer: Lesion of PPRF and MLF (one-and-a-half syndrome)
row.Reference: One-and-a-Half Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The one-and-a-half syndrome is a rare but distinct disorder of ocular motility resulting from a lesion affecting the pontine paramedian reticular formation (PPRF) or the abducens nucleus on one side, combined with an injury to the ipsilateral medial longitudinal fasciculus (MLF). Clinically, it presents with a complete loss of horizontal gaze to one side (due to PPRF/abducens nucleus lesion) and an ipsilateral internuclear ophthalmoplegia (INO) when looking to the other side (due to MLF lesion). This means one eye can only abduct (the contralateral eye in the direction of the intact PPRF), while the other eye cannot move horizontally at all.

row.Question:
What is the significance of positive Babinski sign with muscle atrophy and fasciculations in the same limb?
a) Pure lower motor neuron lesion
b) Combined upper and lower motor neuron lesion (e.g., ALS)
c) Brainstem stroke
d) Multiple sclerosis
e) Functional disorder
row.Text Answer: Combined upper and lower motor neuron lesion (e.g., ALS)
row.Reference: Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis (ALS) - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The simultaneous presence of upper motor neuron (UMN) signs, such as a positive Babinski sign and brisk reflexes, alongside lower motor neuron (LMN) signs, including muscle atrophy and fasciculations, in the same limb or body region is the hallmark of a disease affecting both motor neuron systems. This clinical picture is most characteristic of amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS).

row.Question:
A patient has homonymous upper quadrantanopia and fluent aphasia. How many lesions are needed to explain this?
a) 1 lesion
b) 2 lesions
c) 1 lesion in the dominant temporal lobe (Meyer's loop + Wernicke’s area)
d) 3 lesions
e) 2 lesions in separate hemispheres
row.Text Answer: 1 lesion in the dominant temporal lobe (Meyer's loop + Wernicke’s area)
row.Reference: Blumenfeld, H. (2010). Neuroanatomy through Clinical Cases (2nd ed.). Sinauer Associates
row.Context: Fluent (Wernicke's) aphasia is caused by lesions in Wernicke's area, located in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the dominant hemisphere. The optic radiations forming Meyer's loop, which transmit information for the contralateral upper visual field, also course through the temporal lobe. Therefore, a single lesion in the dominant temporal lobe can encompass both Wernicke's area and Meyer's loop, explaining the co-occurrence of fluent aphasia and a contralateral homonymous upper quadrantanopia

row.Question:
What is the appropriate action when a young woman starts oral contraceptives and her blood pressure rises from 120/80 to 160/110 after 6 weeks?
a) Switch to a different contraceptive
b) Discontinue the contraceptive
c) Add antihypertensive therapy
d) Monitor for another 6 weeks
e) Reduce salt intake
row.Reference: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists (ACOG) Practice Bulletin No. 195: Counseling About Contraception for Women With Medical Conditions (Reaffirmed 2021).
row.Context: Although less common with modern low-dose formulations, oral contraceptives can induce or exacerbate hypertension in susceptible individuals. If a woman develops significant or sustained hypertension (e.g., blood pressure consistently ≥ 160/100 mmHg) while on oral contraceptives, the oral contraceptive should be discontinued immediately. Other forms of contraception should be considered, and the patient's blood pressure should be re-evaluated after cessation of the hormonal therapy. Antihypertensive medications may be initiated if blood pressure remains elevated after discontinuation of the oral contraceptive.

row.Question:
What are the most reliable diagnostic tests for diabetes mellitus?
a) HbA1c and urinalysis
b) Family history and symptoms
c) Fasting plasma glucose, OGTT, and HbA1c
d) Random blood glucose only
e) Physical examination
row.Text Answer: Fasting plasma glucose, OGTT, and HbA1c
row.Reference: Classification and Diagnosis of Diabetes: Standards of Medical Care in Diabetes—2024. Diabetes Care.
row.Context: The diagnosis of diabetes can be made based on plasma glucose criteria, including fasting plasma glucose (FPG), 2-hour plasma glucose (2-h PG) during a 75-g oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT), or random plasma glucose (in an individual with classic symptoms of hyperglycemia or hyperglycemic crisis). Additionally, a hemoglobin A1c (HbA1c) level of ≥6.5% is also a diagnostic criterion. These tests reflect different aspects of glucose metabolism and are considered the primary methods for diagnosing diabetes.

row.Question:
A 77-year-old woman presents with sudden bilateral blindness and asymmetric paraparesis with a T4 sensory level. What is the likely diagnosis?
a) Anterior spinal artery syndrome
b) Neuromyelitis optica (Devic’s disease)
c) Multiple sclerosis
d) Bilateral occipital infarcts
e) Transverse myelitis
row.Reference: Neuromyelitis Optica Spectrum Disorder (NMOSD) - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Neuromyelitis optica spectrum disorder (NMOSD), historically known as Devic's disease, is a rare, severe, relapsing inflammatory demyelinating disease of the central nervous system. Its cardinal clinical manifestations include optic neuritis, which can be severe and bilateral (leading to acute visual loss or blindness), and acute transverse myelitis, characterized by motor weakness (like paraparesis), sensory disturbances with a distinct sensory level, and often bladder/bowel dysfunction. The combination of acute, severe optic nerve involvement and acute myelitis strongly points to NMOSD, even in older adults.

row.Question:
Which infection-related disease presents with cerebellar ataxia, hemiplegia, and multiple cranial nerve palsies, and may lead to splenic rupture?
a) Cytomegalovirus infection
b) Bacterial meningitis
c) Infectious mononucleosis (EBV)
d) Toxoplasmosis
e) Herpes simplex encephalitis

row.Context: Infectious mononucleosis, caused by the Epstein-Barr virus (EBV), is widely recognized for its systemic manifestations, including significant splenomegaly which carries a well-known risk of splenic rupture, particularly following trauma. While less common, EBV infection can also lead to a variety of neurological complications, presenting as acute cerebellar ataxia, encephalitis (which may involve focal deficits like hemiplegia), and cranial neuropathies (such as multiple cranial nerve palsies)

row.Question:
What condition presents with ipsilateral fixed dilated pupil, contralateral hemiparesis, and is a complication of uncal herniation?
a) Cerebellar stroke
b) Transtentorial herniation
c) Subdural hematoma
d) Central pontine myelinolysis
e) Temporal epilepsy
row.Reference: Brain Herniation - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Transtentorial herniation, particularly the uncal type, is a critical neurological emergency. It is characterized by the compression of the brainstem structures as the uncus of the temporal lobe shifts medially and inferiorly through the tentorial notch. The classic clinical signs include an ipsilateral fixed and dilated pupil (due to compression of the oculomotor nerve's parasympathetic fibers) and contralateral hemiparesis (from compression of the cerebral peduncle, often against the tentorial edge, known as Kernohan's notch phenomenon). These symptoms are directly a complication of the uncal herniation.

row.Question:
What is the most likely diagnosis in a patient with sudden-onset severe headache, neck stiffness, and negative CT scan?
a) Tension-type headache
b) Ischemic stroke
c) Cluster headache
d) Subarachnoid hemorrhage (requires lumbar puncture)
e) Sinusitis
row.Reference: Edlow, J. A., Caplan, L. R., & The Headache Cooperative of New England. (2000). Avoiding an Error: A Case of Thunderclap Headache. Neurology, 55(9)
row.Context: A sudden, severe 'thunderclap' headache is the hallmark symptom of subarachnoid hemorrhage (SAH). Neck stiffness (meningismus) is also a common associated symptom. While non-contrast head CT is the initial imaging modality, a normal CT scan does not reliably exclude SAH, particularly if the CT is performed more than 6-12 hours after symptom onset or if the hemorrhage is small. In such cases, a lumbar puncture to evaluate for xanthochromia in the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) is mandatory to definitively rule out SAH.

row.Question:
What is the best long-term prophylaxis for recurrent deep vein thrombosis in a patient with a known hypercoagulable state?
a) Aspirin 100 mg daily
b) Fondaparinux
c) Warfarin with INR monitoring
d) Clopidogrel
e) Compression stockings only
row.Reference: American Society of Hematology (ASH) 2020 guidelines for the management of venous thromboembolism: treatment of deep vein thrombosis and pulmonary embolism. Blood Advances, 4(19),
row.Context: For patients with a known hypercoagulable state who have experienced a deep vein thrombosis (DVT), long-term anticoagulation is crucial for preventing recurrence. Warfarin, with careful monitoring of the International Normalized Ratio (INR), has historically been the gold standard for long-term oral prophylaxis in these patients. While direct oral anticoagulants (DOACs) are increasingly used and often preferred for their convenience, warfarin remains a highly effective and appropriate choice, particularly in specific hypercoagulable conditions or where DOACs may be contraindicated or less studied.

row.Question:
Which clinical feature distinguishes neuroborreliosis from other causes of facial palsy?
a) Bilateral ptosis
b) Associated skin rash
c) Bilateral facial nerve palsy
d) Hyperacusis
e) Sudden hearing loss
row.Reference: Peripheral Nervous System Involvement in Lyme Disease - PMC - PubMed Central.
row.Context: While idiopathic Bell's palsy is typically unilateral, bilateral facial nerve palsy is a highly characteristic, though not exclusive, manifestation of Lyme neuroborreliosis. Its presence in conjunction with other neurological or systemic symptoms should strongly prompt consideration and testing for Lyme disease, distinguishing it from most other causes of isolated facial palsy.

row.Question:
A patient presents with hemineglect, anosognosia, and constructional apraxia. Which brain region is most likely affected?
a) Dominant frontal lobe
b) Non-dominant parietal lobe
c) Basal ganglia
d) Hippocampus
e) Occipital cortex
row.Reference: Hemispatial Neglect - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: The constellation of neurological deficits including hemineglect (unilateral spatial neglect), anosognosia (lack of awareness of one's deficits), and constructional apraxia is highly characteristic of damage to the non-dominant (typically right) parietal lobe. This region plays a crucial role in spatial attention, body schema, and visuomotor integration, and lesions here impair the patient's ability to attend to, perceive, or act on stimuli in the contralateral (left) space, along with a striking unawareness of their impairments."

row.Question:
What is the most appropriate first step when hypertensive encephalopathy is suspected?
a) MRI of the brain
b) Immediate reduction of blood pressure with IV antihypertensives
c) Start oral beta-blockers
d) Lumbar puncture
e) EEG
row.Text Answer: Immediate reduction of blood pressure with IV antihypertensives
row.Reference: Hypertensive Emergency - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Hypertensive encephalopathy is a true medical emergency characterized by a sudden, severe increase in blood pressure leading to cerebral edema and neurological dysfunction. The immediate and most critical first step in its management is the rapid, controlled reduction of blood pressure using intravenous antihypertensive agents. This is essential to prevent further brain damage and reverse the neurological symptoms

row.Question:
Which symptom is most specific for temporal lobe epilepsy?
a) Visual aura
b) Focal motor seizures
c) Déjà vu sensation and olfactory hallucinations
d) Unilateral tremor
e) Bilateral myoclonus
row.Text Answer: Déjà vu sensation and olfactory hallucinations
row.Reference: Temporal Lobe Epilepsy - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Seizures originating from the temporal lobe, particularly the mesial structures (e.g., hippocampus, amygdala), are frequently heralded by characteristic auras or initial symptoms. These commonly include experiential phenomena such as a déjà vu sensation (a feeling of having previously experienced something that is actually new), and olfactory hallucinations (perceiving smells that are not present, often unpleasant). These symptoms are considered highly specific for the localization of seizure onset within the temporal lobe.

row.Question:
What neurological sign suggests a lesion in the frontal eye field?
a) Pupillary dilatation
b) Gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion
c) Diplopia
d) Nystagmus
e) Downbeat nystagmus
row.Text Answer: Gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion
row.Reference: Gaze Palsies - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf
row.Context: Acute, destructive lesions of the frontal eye fields (FEFs), which are located in the frontal lobe and are responsible for generating contralateral voluntary saccadic eye movements, typically result in conjugate gaze deviation toward the side of the lesion. This occurs because the tonic activity of the intact contralateral FEF pulls the eyes towards the side of the lesion, and the damaged FEF can no longer drive gaze to the opposite side.

row.Question:
Which of the following most accurately localizes a lesion in Brown-Séquard syndrome?
a) Bilateral loss of all modalities below the lesion
b) Ipsilateral motor loss and contralateral loss of pain and temperature
c) Ipsilateral loss of all modalities
d) Contralateral hemiplegia
e) Lower motor neuron signs bilaterally
row.Text Answer: Ipsilateral motor loss and contralateral loss of pain and temperature
row.Reference: Brown-Sequard Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Brown-Séquard syndrome results from a hemisection (damage to one side) of the spinal cord. Classically, it presents with a unique combination of deficits below the level of the lesion: ipsilateral motor loss (due to involvement of the lateral corticospinal tract), ipsilateral loss of proprioception and vibration sense (due to involvement of the dorsal columns), and contralateral loss of pain and temperature sensation (due to involvement of the spinothalamic tract, which crosses immediately upon entering the spinal cord).

row.Question:
A patient presents with right facial weakness, hoarseness, loss of pain and temperature on the left body and right face, and Horner’s syndrome. What is the most likely diagnosis?
a) Medial medullary syndrome
b) Cerebellar stroke
c) Lateral medullary syndrome (Wallenberg syndrome)
d) Multiple sclerosis
e) Bell’s palsy
row.Reference: Wallenberg Syndrome - StatPearls - NCBI Bookshelf.
row.Context: Wallenberg syndrome, or lateral medullary syndrome, is typically caused by an infarct of the posterior inferior cerebellar artery (PICA). It presents with a distinctive constellation of neurological deficits due to damage to structures in the lateral medulla. Key features include ipsilateral (same side as lesion) loss of pain and temperature sensation on the face (spinal trigeminal nucleus and tract), ipsilateral Horner's syndrome (miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis from descending sympathetic fibers), dysphagia and hoarseness (from nucleus ambiguus affecting CN IX and X), vertigo and nystagmus (from vestibular nuclei), and contralateral (opposite side as lesion) loss of pain and temperature sensation on the body (spinothalamic tract). While facial weakness is not a universal component, it can sometimes be present if the lesion extends to involve the facial nucleus or its exiting fibers

CRISPR‐ABE editing of the PCSK9 D374Y allele in hepatocytes can permanently convert the aspartate codon 374 to asparagine (D374N), restoring normal auto‐inhibitory binding to LDLR and enhancing LDLR recycling; unlike inclisiran (transient RNAi) or evolocumab (antibody clearance), ABE achieves allele‐specific correction but is limited by potential off‐target adenine deamination in APOB and ANGPTL4 loci.
B. CRISPR‐ABE introduces a premature stop codon at codon 374 (D374X), leading to nonsense‐mediated decay of PCSK9 mRNA; this builds permanent loss‐of‐function, bypassing the need for LDLR entirely via upregulated LRP1 receptor clearance. Inclisiran and evolocumab only reduce secreted PCSK9 temporarily and cannot address D374Y’s increased affinity for LDLR.
C. In vivo CRISPR‐ABE editing targets the PCSK9 promoter’s sterol‐regulatory element (SRE), lowering PCSK9 transcription by preventing SREBP2 binding; this epigenetic change is heritable in hepatocyte lineages. Inclisiran acts post-transcriptionally and is reversible, while evolocumab only neutralizes circulating PCSK9 but cannot alter transcription.
D. CRISPR‐ABE precisely converts the D374Y codon to D374‐silencing D374Y via an A→G base edit, thus eliminating the gain‐of‐function protein. This results in up‐regulation of residual LDLR activity, but because the patient is homozygous null for LDLR, LDLR‐dependent clearance remains absent. In contrast, inclisiran and evolocumab lower both wild‐type and D374Y PCSK9, modestly upregulating LRP1–mediated VLDL remnant clearance as a compensatory mechanism.
E. CRISPR‐ABE editing of hepatocyte PCSK9 results in partial loss of function, exposing a neoepitope that leads to immunogenic clearance of edited hepatocytes; thus, although allele‐specific, it has high immunotoxicity risk. Inclisiran and evolocumab, by contrast, avoid immunotoxicity but cannot permanently suppress D374Y’s exaggerated binding to LDLR, requiring lifelong dosing.

row.Context: “CRISPR adenine base editors of PCSK9 were confirmed in primary human hepatocytes, primary monkey hepatocytes, and mice. In vivo CRISPR ABE delivery led to a near-complete knockdown of PCSK9 in the liver after a single infusion of lipid nanoparticles (LNPs), with concomitant reductions in blood levels of PCSK9 and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol of approximately 90% and about 60%, respectively; all of these changes remained stable for at least 8 months after a single-dose treatment. No relevant side effects were observed in the animals treated with a CRISPR editor-based strategy, and off-target gene editing was found at only one site in macaque liver, whereas no off-target editing was detected in human hepatocytes.”
